forces: Concert band; transcription by Lawrence Odom
performers: United States Air Force Band, Concert Band
intro: The United States Air Force Band plays the first movement of La Mer in Lawrence Odom’s concert-band arrangement. A low B, barely stirring, grows into the broad D♭-major chords of noon.

sections.label: Intro · Dawn over a low B
sections.mNote: Short phrases emerge above a held bass note

sections.label: A · D♭ major, a flowing pulse
sections.mNote: Six quavers to the bar, with quick figures underneath

sections.label: B · Rising figures and answering phrases
sections.mNote: Short phrases overlap above the moving accompaniment

sections.label: C · A melody in four parts
sections.mNote: Four interwoven lines carry the new tune

sections.label: D · Short phrases, softer answers
sections.mNote: The melody breaks into shorter exchanges

sections.label: Link · Held notes before the chorale
sections.mNote: Long notes and quiet phrases prepare the slower close

sections.label: E · The phrases broaden
sections.mNote: The closing tune gathers over continuing movement

sections.label: Coda · The noon chorale
sections.mNote: Broad chords bring the movement home to D♭

cues.title: Dawn on B
cues.text: A low B lies beneath the opening. Small phrases emerge above it, with long spaces between them. Debussy writes Très lent — very slow — and lets the first few notes arrive almost one by one.
cues.evidence: Debussy, La Mer, Durand full score, opening, printed pp. 143–145. The harmony and pacing belong to the composition; instrumental assignments in Odom’s transcription are omitted. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/b/b6/IMSLP15420-Debussy_-_La_Mer_%28orch._score%29.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The sea from Burgundy
cues.text: In the summer of 1903 Debussy is staying with his parents-in-law in Burgundy, far from the coast. He begins La Mer there, drawing on memories of childhood summers at Cannes.
cues.evidence: Composition in Burgundy: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_mer_(Debussy). Childhood visits to Cannes: Jacob Greenberg’s Boston Symphony programme note, https://www.bso.org/works/la-mer

cues.title: Six quavers, without heaviness
cues.text: The main movement settles into D♭ major and 6/8. Debussy marks it Modéré, sans lenteur: moderate, without slowness. The little rising phrases now have a running accompaniment beneath them.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, printed p. 147: change to five flats and 6/8, Modéré, sans lenteur, with continuous semiquavers.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Hokusai on the cover
cues.text: Debussy chooses Hokusai’s The Great Wave off Kanagawa for the cover of the published score. The curling wave becomes the first image readers see when they pick up La Mer.
cues.evidence: Debussy’s choice of Hokusai for the score is documented by Jacob Greenberg, https://www.bso.org/works/la-mer. The print and score cover are reproduced at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_mer_(Debussy).

cues.title: Two against three
cues.text: Groups of two notes and groups of three keep crossing through this movement. One phrase divides the beat evenly while another leans across it. Even a quiet passage can have this small rhythmic tug inside it.
cues.evidence: Jacob Greenberg identifies the persistent interplay of twos and threes throughout the first movement: https://www.bso.org/works/la-mer
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: Four lines, one tune
cues.text: A new melody opens out in four parts, marked Très rythmé — strongly rhythmic. Its lines rise and answer one another, making a much longer sentence than the little calls of the opening.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, rehearsal 9, printed p. 161: the four-part melody. The note describes the written music without assigning Odom’s parts to particular instruments.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Debussy takes the podium
cues.text: Camille Chevillard conducts the première in Paris on 15 October 1905, to a cool reception. In January 1908 Debussy conducts it himself. This time the Paris audience is won over.
cues.evidence: Jacob Greenberg’s Boston Symphony programme note gives the première and Debussy’s Paris performances on 19 and 26 January 1908: https://www.bso.org/works/la-mer

cues.title: The noon chorale
cues.text: The closing chorale moves in broad notes, with quicker figures still flowing underneath. The score returns to Très lent. D♭ major, first reached after the introduction, now fills the ending.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, rehearsal 14 to the end of movement I, printed pp. 171–173: Très lent, chorale and D♭-major close.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: B opens into D♭
transitions.from: Intro · Dawn over a low B
transitions.to: A · D♭ major, a flowing pulse
transitions.how: The opening’s B-centred harmony shifts into D♭ major. Debussy changes from 6/4 to 6/8 and writes Modéré, sans lenteur. The sustained bass and widely spaced calls become short phrases over continuous semiquavers; the pulse begins to flow.
transitions.evidence: Durand full score, printed pp. 146–147, from the accelerating introduction into the main 6/8. This describes the composition’s harmony and rhythm, without assigning instruments in the transcription.

transitions.title: The tune becomes a chorale
transitions.how: At Très lent, the chorale stretches across the bar in broad, sustained notes. Quicker figures continue below it, so the movement carries two speeds at once. The closing progression gathers around D♭ major and ends with short, emphatic chords.
transitions.evidence: Durand full score, rehearsal 14 to the end of movement I, printed pp. 171–173. The description is restricted to the musical writing shared by the original and the transcription.

composer.epithet: He trusted his ear over the rules — “pleasure is the law” — and made the piano, the flute and the orchestra sound new.
facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1872; piano with Antoine Marmontel, composition with Ernest Guiraud
Prix de Rome 1884 · Paris Exposition 1889 · Pelléas et Mélisande 1902
One completed opera, orchestral triptychs, piano collections, songs, a quartet and three late sonatas
Symbolist poetry · Mussorgsky · the Javanese gamelan · Couperin and Rameau
composer.background:
Debussy was born above his parents’ china shop in Saint-Germain-en-Laye, west of Paris, on 22 August 1862. His parents were not musicians. His father fought for the Paris Commune in 1871 and went to prison for it, and there he met Charles de Sivry, whose mother, Antoinette Mauté, taught the piano and said she had been a pupil of Chopin. She took the boy on. In 1872, aged ten, he entered the Paris Conservatoire.

His teachers could not make him out. Antoine Marmontel, his piano professor, found “a charming child, a truly artistic temperament” in January 1874; the harmony teacher Émile Durand reported in June 1879 that he was “very gifted in harmony, but hopelessly unfocused”. Years later, discussing chords at the piano with his old composition teacher Ernest Guiraud around 1890, he put his position plainly: “There is no theory. You merely have to listen. Pleasure is the law.”
